entities.summary:
Percy Clinton Sydney Smythe, 6th Viscount Strangford, was a British diplomat who played a crucial role in shaping the country's foreign policy during the mid-19th century. Born into the aristocracy, Smythe was educated at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, before entering the diplomatic service. He served as the British ambassador to the Netherlands from 1841 to 1845, where he negotiated the Anglo-Dutch Treaty, which helped to resolve a long-standing trade dispute between the two nations.

Smythe's diplomatic career was marked by his ability to navigate complex international relationships and negotiate favorable treaties. He also played a key role in the establishment of the London Conference, a gathering of European diplomats that aimed to resolve the Great Eastern Question, a complex dispute over the control of the Suez Canal.

Despite his significant contributions to British foreign policy, Smythe's legacy is often overshadowed by that of his contemporaries. However, his work in the diplomatic service helped to establish the United Kingdom as a major player in international relations, paving the way for Britain's emergence as a global superpower in the 20th century.

In his later years, Smythe was remembered for his wit and charm, which he used to great effect in his diplomatic dealings. He was also known for his love of horses and his extensive collection of horses, which he amassed during his travels.

Smythe's story serves as a reminder of the often-overlooked role that diplomats play in shaping the course of history. His legacy is a testament to the enduring power of diplomacy in resolving conflicts and building relationships between nations.
